title: The Subjunctive
subtitle: λύω, λύῃς, λύῃ — the mood of uncertainty and purpose.
objectives: Form and conjugate the present and aorist subjunctive in all voices.
Understand the subjunctive as the mood of uncertainty, purpose, and exhortation.
Use the subjunctive in hortatory, deliberative, and purpose clauses.
Distinguish subjunctive from indicative by form and meaning.

sections.heading: The subjunctive mood
sections.body:
The subjunctive is the mood of uncertainty and purpose. It expresses what may happen, what should happen, or what is aimed at. The indicative states facts; the subjunctive expresses possibilities, commands, purposes.

The subjunctive is formed with lengthened thematic vowels: ω/η instead of ο/ε. The present subjunctive uses the present stem; the aorist subjunctive uses the aorist stem (without the augment). The future has no subjunctive.

The subjunctive has no time reference. The present subjunctive does not mean present time; the aorist subjunctive does not mean past time. Both can refer to future or general time. The difference between present and aorist subjunctive is aspect: present = ongoing action, aorist = completed action.

sections.heading: The present subjunctive active: λύω, λύῃς, λύῃ
sections.body:
singular
  1st   λύω         (that) I may loose
  2nd   λύῃς        (that) you may loose
  3rd   λύῃ         (that) he/she/it may loose

  plural
  1st   λύωμεν      (that) we may loose
  2nd   λύητε       (that) you (plural) may loose
  3rd   λύωσι(ν)    (that) they may loose

The endings are -ω, -ῃς, -ῃ, -ωμεν, -ητε, -ωσι. The long vowels ω/η distinguish the subjunctive from the indicative.

sections.heading: The aorist subjunctive active: λύσω, λύσῃς, λύσῃ
sections.body:
singular
  1st   λύσω        (that) I may loose
  2nd   λύσῃς       (that) you may loose
  3rd   λύσῃ        (that) he/she/it may loose

  plural
  1st   λύσωμεν     (that) we may loose
  2nd   λύσητε      (that) you (plural) may loose
  3rd   λύσωσι(ν)   (that) they may loose

No augment. The aorist stem λυσ- + subjunctive endings. The aorist subjunctive looks like the future indicative, but without time reference.

sections.heading: Uses of the subjunctive
sections.body:
Hortatory: λύωμεν τοὺς αἰχμαλώτους — 'Let us free the prisoners.' First person plural subjunctive used as a command.

Deliberative: τί ποιῶμεν; — 'What should we do?' Subjunctive in a question expressing doubt or deliberation.

Purpose clause with ἵνα: ἔρχομαι ἵνα λύσω τοὺς αἰχμαλώτους — 'I come in order that I may free the prisoners.' ἵνα + subjunctive = purpose.

Fear clause with μή: φοβοῦμαι μὴ ἔλθωσιν — 'I fear that they may come.' μή + subjunctive after verbs of fearing.

items.prompt: First person singular present subjunctive active of λύω
First person plural aorist subjunctive active of λύω
What distinguishes the subjunctive from the indicative?
items.answer: The long thematic vowels ω/η instead of ο/ε.

items.prompt: Translate: ἔρχομαι ἵνα λύσω τοὺς αἰχμαλώτους.
items.answer: I come in order that I may free the prisoners.

items.prompt: Does the aorist subjunctive refer to past time?
items.answer: No. The subjunctive has no time reference.

words.gloss: I come in order to free the prisoners.

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Lesson 4.2 introduces the optative. The optative is the mood of wish and remote possibility. λύοιμι means 'may I loose' or 'I might loose'. The optative is rarer than the subjunctive, but it is essential for understanding classical Greek.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark the lesson complete when you can conjugate the present and aorist subjunctive of any ω-verb and can translate hortatory, deliberative, and purpose clauses correctly.
